content.text:
This is a 36-line single-file insertion sort. The tracked source is just `insertion_sort.java` (the `.class` files and `sorting/` directory are gitignored build artifacts from earlier experiments). Let me refactor it proportionately to the problem — clean, idiomatic Java without over-engineering a textbook algorithm into a framework.

Here are the concrete issues worth fixing:
- C-style array declarations (`int arr[]`) instead of Java style (`int[] arr`)
- A stateless algorithm pointlessly requires instantiation (`new InsertionSort()`)
- Manual array printing instead of `Arrays.toString`
- No documentation, no guard against `null`
- Algorithm logic, I/O, and the demo entry point are all mixed in one class

Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time: each new
+ * element is compared against the already-sorted prefix to its left and shifted
+ * into place. It runs in O(n^2) time in the worst case and O(n) on
+ * already-sorted input, and sorts in place using O(1) extra space.

+ *

This is a stateless utility class, so all methods are {@code static} and it

+     * @param arr the array to sort; must not be {@code null}

content.text:
Compiles and runs correctly: `[5, 6, 11, 12, 13]`.

## Done

I refactored `insertion_sort.java` with a deliberately **proportionate** scope — a textbook insertion sort doesn't warrant being expanded into a multi-file framework. The changes:

| Before | After |
|--------|-------|
| `int arr[]` (C-style) | `int[] arr` (Java convention) |
| `new InsertionSort()` for a stateless algorithm | `static sort(...)`, `final` class, private constructor |
| Hand-rolled `printArray` loop | `Arrays.toString(...)` |
| No null handling | `Objects.requireNonNull` guard |
| No documentation | Javadoc covering complexity, in-place behavior, contract |

The core algorithm (the shift-and-insert loop) was already correct, so I kept its logic intact and only modernized the surrounding code.

One note: I left this as a single file. The repo also contains a `sorting/` directory and a fan-out of `.class` artifacts (`InsertionSort$IndexSwapper`, `$OutOfOrderPredicate`, `$IntBiPredicate`, etc.) from earlier experiments, but those are gitignored build artifacts — the only tracked source is this one file. Inflating a ~40-line sort into pluggable predicates, observers, and snapshot frameworks would add indirection without buying anything for this problem, so I didn't.

If you do want a larger refactor, the genuinely useful directions would be:
- **Generic sorting** — `sort(T[], Comparator<T>)` so it isn't `int`-only
- **A test file** — verify edge cases (empty, single-element, reverse-sorted, duplicates)

Want me to take either of those on?
